video_title: Binary Search — The Algorithm That Finds Anything in 24 Steps
video_hook: If you had to find one user in a database of 10 million, checking one by one would take 10 million steps. But there's a trick that does it in just 24.
open_loop_question: Why does cutting the search space in half feel almost unfairly powerful?
retention_beats: Here is the part most people miss.
This is where the speedup happens.
suggested_youtube_title: Binary Search Explained — Find Anything in a Billion Records (Visual Guide)

scenes.title: The Problem
scenes.narration: Imagine you have a sorted list of 10 million users. You need to find one specific name. Checking each one, one by one, could take 10 million steps. But there's a trick that finds the answer in about 24 steps. How? That's what we'll figure out.
scenes.visual_description: Large number emphasis, then curiosity text.

actions.title: The Challenge
actions.body:
Find one name in a sorted list of 10 million entries.
Brute force: check every single one.
Can we do better?

scenes.title: The Naive Approach: Linear Search
scenes.narration: Let's try the obvious way first. Start at the beginning and check each element. The target is 72. We check 3, then 8, then 15, then 22... we're not even close. This is linear search — it works, but it's painfully slow.
scenes.visual_description: Table with array, highlight moves row by row, shake on slow realization.

scenes.title: Linear Search Is Slow
scenes.narration: Here is the part most people miss. With 10 million elements, linear search averages 5 million comparisons. That's O of n. Can we do dramatically better?
scenes.visual_description: Shake the table to show frustration, then show O(n) math.

scenes.title: The Key Insight: Divide and Conquer
scenes.narration: What if the list is sorted? Then we can do something clever. Instead of starting from the beginning, start in the middle. If the middle value is too big, throw away the entire right half. If it's too small, throw away the left half. Each step cuts the problem in half.
scenes.visual_description: Emphasize the key insight, then bullet list of the idea.

actions.text: Cut in half. Every. Single. Time.

actions.title: Binary Search — Core Idea
items: Start in the middle of the sorted array
Too big? Discard the right half
Too small? Discard the left half

scenes.title: Step 1: Find the Middle
scenes.narration: Now watch what changes. Our sorted array has 9 elements. The middle index is 4, and the value there is 34. Our target is 72. Since 72 is greater than 34, we know the answer must be in the right half. We throw away indexes 0 through 4.
scenes.visual_description: Full table, middle highlighted, dim left half.

scenes.title: Step 2: Narrow the Range
scenes.narration: This is where the speedup happens. Our range is now indexes 5 to 8. The new middle is index 6, value 55. Since 72 is greater than 55, we discard the left side again. Half the data — gone in one comparison.

scenes.title: Step 3: Almost There
scenes.narration: Now we only have indexes 7 and 8 left. The middle is index 7, value 67. Still less than 72, so we move right one more time.

scenes.title: Step 4: Found!
scenes.narration: Here is the hidden trick paying off. Index 8, value 72. That's our target! Found in just 4 steps instead of 9. And with 10 million elements? Only 24 steps.
scenes.visual_description: Final step, target found, big emphasis.

scenes.title: Edge Case: Target Not Found
scenes.narration: But what if the target isn't in the array? Say we search for 50. We'd narrow down to an empty range. Binary search handles this gracefully — when the low pointer passes the high pointer, we know the element doesn't exist.
scenes.visual_description: Search for missing element, show empty range.

scenes.title: The Code
scenes.narration: Here's the pseudocode. We maintain two pointers, low and high. Each iteration, we compute the middle, compare, and adjust. The loop runs at most log-base-2 of n times. Simple, elegant, and devastatingly efficient.

scenes.title: Why O(log n) Is Powerful
scenes.narration: This is where the speedup happens. The complexity is O of log n. For 10 million elements, log base 2 of 10 million is about 23.25. So at most 24 comparisons. Compare that to 10 million for linear search.

scenes.title: Where It's Used
scenes.narration: This is why real systems care about this. Binary search powers database indexes, autocomplete suggestions, spelling checkers, git bisect for finding bugs, and even the way your browser finds cookies. It's everywhere.

actions.title: Binary Search in the Real World
items: Database indexes (B-trees use the same principle)
Git bisect — find the commit that broke your code
Binary search on the answer (competitive programming)

scenes.title: The Answer
scenes.narration: So why does cutting in half feel unfairly powerful? Because each step doesn't remove one element — it removes HALF of everything that's left. After 24 halving steps, 10 million becomes 1. That's the magic of logarithms. And that's binary search.

actions.title: Key Takeaways
items: Each step eliminates half the remaining elements
One of the most important algorithms in CS
